clinicalPearls: Pain is characteristically out of proportion to visible skin changes and may be delayed for hours, especially after exposure to dilute solutions
Unlike other acids, the danger is the fluoride ion rather than the hydrogen ion, so injury and systemic toxicity extend well beyond the surface burn
Fingertip and nail-bed burns are common and notoriously painful, often with minimal early skin findings
Systemic fluoride absorption chelates calcium and magnesium, causing hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia that can precipitate life-threatening arrhythmias
Hyperkalaemia from cellular efflux is an additional driver of cardiotoxicity in significant exposures
Copious irrigation followed by calcium therapy is the cornerstone of treatment, with topical, local or intra-arterial calcium used depending on site and severity
Inhalational and large or concentrated dermal exposures warrant cardiac monitoring and aggressive correction of electrolyte disturbance
Any ingestion or large surface-area or high-concentration exposure should prompt early poisons-centre discussion and monitoring for systemic toxicity
reference.pathophysiology: Hydrofluoric acid is a relatively weak acid, so surface corrosion is often modest, but the fluoride ion penetrates deeply into tissue. There it binds avidly to calcium and magnesium, forming insoluble salts that cause liquefactive necrosis and intense, progressive pain. The resulting fall in ionised calcium and magnesium disrupts cellular function and cardiac conduction, while fluoride also promotes potassium efflux from cells. The combination of hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hyperkalaemia predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias, which are the usual cause of death in serious systemic poisoning.
additionalDifferentials: Other acid or alkali chemical burns
additionalInvestigations: Serum ionised calcium, magnesium and potassium with serial monitoring
Electrocardiogram and continuous cardiac monitoring for QT prolongation and arrhythmia
Arterial blood gas and renal function in significant exposures
Assessment of burn depth, surface area and involved sites
redFlags: Ingestion, inhalation or large or high-concentration dermal exposure
Severe or worsening pain disproportionate to skin appearance
Involvement of the face, airway or extensive body surface area
reference.prognosis: Small dilute dermal burns treated promptly with irrigation and calcium usually heal well, but concentrated, extensive, inhalational or ingested exposures can cause refractory electrolyte disturbance and fatal arrhythmia despite treatment.
pitfalls: Underestimating severity because the surface burn looks trivial
Failing to anticipate and correct hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hyperkalaemia
Not instituting cardiac monitoring after significant exposure
Treating it like an ordinary acid burn and omitting calcium therapy
Discharging a patient with fingertip burns before ensuring adequate pain control and follow-up
